BIO 30 · Unit C

How can cells preserve, recombine, express, and change genetic information?

Move from chromosome behaviour to inheritance probabilities, DNA expression, mutation, biotechnology, and evidence-based genetic decisions.

Required learning
40.0 hours
Lessons
24
Portfolio artifacts
12

Learning intention

I am learning to use models and evidence to explain cell Division, Genetics, and Molecular Biology.

Success criteria

  • I can trace chromosomes through mitosis and meiosis and connect their behaviour to inheritance patterns.
  • I can solve genetic problems, analyze pedigrees and molecular evidence, and state model limits.
  • I can explain DNA replication and expression and evaluate biotechnology evidence, uncertainty, and social implications.

The learning journey

Every lesson begins with a phenomenon, develops a scientific explanation in short sections, makes the mechanism visible in an original semantic model, tests reasoning with a local evidence interaction, and saves a concise exit response. Required learning works without internet access.

Lesson 1 · Cell Division

Chromosomes, Ploidy, and the Cell Cycle

How does chromosome organization preserve information through cell division?

Required time
90 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C1.1k, C1.2k

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to connect chromosome structure, ploidy, DNA replication, and cell-cycle stages.

Success criteria

  • I can distinguish chromatin, a replicated chromosome, a chromatid, a homologous pair, and a chromosome set.
  • I can track DNA amount and chromosome number without counting chromatids as separate chromosomes.
  • I can explain how checkpoints connect growth conditions and DNA integrity to division.

Retrieve

Count by centromeres

A chromosome replicates into two sister chromatids. Has the chromosome number doubled? Explain the counting rule.

Not saved yet

Information package

Chromosomes organize long DNA molecules

A eukaryotic chromosome is one DNA molecule with associated proteins before replication. Chromatin changes compaction across the cell cycle. Genes occupy loci, while homologous chromosomes carry corresponding loci inherited from different parents. Homologues may carry different alleles and are not identical copies.

Name the level being counted. A chromosome count uses centromeres, DNA amount reflects replication, and a homologous-pair count describes chromosome sets. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Ploidy

Chromosome sets and DNA copies are different quantities

Diploid cells contain two homologous chromosome sets, while haploid cells contain one. Replication doubles DNA and creates sister chromatids but does not change ploidy. Fertilization combines two haploid sets, and meiosis reduces a diploid lineage to haploid products.

Use n for chromosome sets only when the organism and stage are clear. Avoid using n as a substitute for total DNA amount. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Cell cycle

Interphase is active preparation

G1 includes growth and normal cell activity, S phase copies DNA, and G2 includes further preparation and repair before M phase. Cells can also enter non-dividing states. Interphase is not cellular rest; transcription, metabolism, growth, replication, and checkpoint control occur there.

A pulse-labelled DNA precursor appears mainly in S-phase cells. Cell counts across phases can estimate relative duration only when sampling assumptions are met. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Control

Checkpoints reduce propagation of damage

Checkpoint systems integrate DNA damage, replication completion, chromosome attachment, cell size, and external growth signals. Cyclins, cyclin-dependent kinases, tumour suppressors, repair pathways, and programmed cell death contribute to regulation. Cancer can involve multiple accumulated changes rather than one universal switch.

A checkpoint delay is evidence that progression changed; it does not identify the exact molecule without targeted measurements. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Chromosome-count evidence model

Compare cells with the same ploidy but different DNA amounts.

Choose a case and report chromosome number, chromatid state, and ploidy separately.

G1 model

Evidence
A diploid model cell has 8 centromeres and each chromosome contains one chromatid.
Explanation
The cell has 8 chromosomes, 8 chromatids, and two chromosome sets.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Count centromeres for chromosomes, count chromatids for DNA copies, and identify sets for ploidy.

  • G1 model: A diploid model cell has 8 centromeres and each chromosome contains one chromatid. The cell has 8 chromosomes, 8 chromatids, and two chromosome sets.
  • G2 model: The same cell has copied its DNA; 8 centromeres connect 16 sister chromatids. The cell still has 8 chromosomes and remains diploid, while DNA and chromatid number have doubled.
  • Gamete model: A mature model gamete contains 4 unreplicated chromosomes. The gamete is haploid because it contains one set; chromosome and chromatid counts are both 4 in this stage.

Lesson 2 · Cell Division

Mitosis and Cytokinesis

How does one nucleus become two genetically equivalent nuclei?

Required time
95 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C1.2k, C1.2s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to explain how mitosis and cytokinesis produce two genetically equivalent nuclei and cells.

Success criteria

  • I can sequence prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, and cytokinesis by chromosome evidence.
  • I can explain spindle attachment and sister-chromatid separation without saying chromosomes choose where to move.
  • I can compare plant and animal cytokinesis and state what genetic equivalence does not mean.

Retrieve

Equivalent is not unchanged

How can daughter cells be genetically equivalent yet later develop different structures or functions?

Not saved yet

Preparation

Chromosomes condense and the spindle forms

During prophase and prometaphase, replicated chromosomes condense, centrosome-associated microtubules organize a spindle, the nuclear envelope breaks down, and kinetochores become accessible. Each sister chromatid has a kinetochore associated with its centromere region.

Stage labels summarize continuous changes. Identify a stage from several observations rather than one memorized picture. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Alignment

Metaphase tests bi-orientation

At metaphase, replicated chromosomes align near the cell equator. Sister kinetochores should connect to opposite spindle poles. The spindle-assembly checkpoint delays anaphase until attachments support balanced segregation.

A chromosome at the equator is not waiting by intention; forces and checkpoint signalling emerge from microtubule-kinetochore interactions. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Separation

Sister chromatids become daughter chromosomes

At anaphase, cohesion between sister chromatids is released. Kinetochore microtubules shorten and spindle geometry changes, moving daughter chromosomes toward opposite poles. Once sisters separate, each chromatid is counted as an independent chromosome.

Track centromeres before and after separation to avoid saying chromosome number disappears or permanently doubles. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Completion

Nuclei reform and the cytoplasm divides

Telophase includes chromosome decondensation and nuclear-envelope reformation. Cytokinesis divides cytoplasm. Animal cells commonly use an actin-myosin contractile ring and cleavage furrow; plant cells assemble vesicles into a cell plate that becomes new wall and membrane structures.

Genetic equivalence means the intended chromosome complement is copied, not that mutations never occur or that daughter cells must express the same genes forever. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Mitosis evidence sequencer

Identify stages from chromosome, spindle, and membrane evidence.

Choose a micrograph description and justify its stage.

Aligned chromosomes

Evidence
Condensed duplicated chromosomes form one equatorial line with bipolar attachments.
Explanation
The evidence fits metaphase after attachment and before sister separation.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Use chromosome state, spindle relation, nuclear envelope, and cell-partition evidence for each stage.

  • Aligned chromosomes: Condensed duplicated chromosomes form one equatorial line with bipolar attachments. The evidence fits metaphase after attachment and before sister separation.
  • Two moving groups: Centromeres have separated and V-shaped daughter chromosomes move toward opposite poles. The defining evidence is sister-chromatid separation, so the stage is anaphase.
  • Cell partition: Two nuclei are visible while a plant cell plate grows across the centre. The nuclei have reformed and plant cytokinesis is partitioning the cytoplasm.

Lesson 3 · Cell Division

Cell-Cycle Investigation and Cancer

What can cell counts reveal about cycle timing and loss of regulation?

Required time
105 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C1.2k, C1.1sts, C1.1s, C1.2s, C1.3s, C1.4s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to investigate cell-cycle timing and connect regulation evidence to cancer without reducing cancer to one cause.

Success criteria

  • I can estimate a mitotic index from counted cells and explain the sampling assumptions.
  • I can distinguish correlation, checkpoint mechanism, and causal evidence.
  • I can explain cancer as evolving cell populations with multiple possible regulatory changes.

Retrieve

A snapshot can estimate time

Why can the fraction of cells observed in mitosis estimate relative phase duration only under particular assumptions?

Not saved yet

Investigation

Cell counts become a mitotic index

A mitotic index is the proportion of sampled cells visibly in mitosis: mitotic cells divided by total counted cells. In a large, asynchronously dividing, approximately steady population, a larger phase fraction can suggest more time spent in that phase. Sampling location and cell identification strongly affect the estimate.

Report raw counts, calculation, tissue region, classification rules, uncertainty, and repeated fields. A high index can reflect faster entry, slower mitosis, altered cell loss, or selection of an actively growing region. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Regulation

Cell-cycle control integrates positive and negative signals

Cyclin-CDK activity promotes transitions, while checkpoint proteins, DNA repair, growth-factor pathways, contact conditions, and programmed cell death can delay or stop progression. Tumour suppressors and proto-oncogenes describe normal regulatory roles; mutations can reduce restraints or create inappropriate growth signals.

One gene does not control every cancer. Different tissues and tumours can reach uncontrolled growth through different combinations and sequences of change. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Cancer evolution

Tumours are changing cell populations

Cells within a tumour can differ genetically and phenotypically. Variants that survive, proliferate, avoid immune removal, obtain resources, invade, or resist treatment may become more common. This somatic evolution helps explain heterogeneity, progression, and treatment resistance.

A mutation found in a tumour can be a driver, a passenger, or a later consequence. Frequency, timing, function, and experimental evidence help distinguish roles. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Responsible claims

Cell models do not diagnose a person

Microscope counts and cultured-cell evidence can test mechanisms but do not establish a diagnosis or treatment plan. Cancer risk and outcome depend on tissue, inherited and acquired variants, exposure, age, immune context, screening, access to care, and many other factors.

Use current authoritative sources and person-centred language. Avoid implying that cancer reflects a personal failure to regulate cells or make correct choices. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Mitotic-index data lab

Compare synthetic tissues with equal sample size but different phase counts.

Choose a sample and distinguish description from mechanism.

Growing root region

Evidence
Eighty of 400 sampled cells are visibly in mitosis across representative fields.
Explanation
The mitotic index is 0.20; active growth is plausible, while phase duration and cell loss still affect interpretation.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Show counts, index, sampling plan, variation, alternative mechanisms, and no-diagnosis boundary.

  • Growing root region: Eighty of 400 sampled cells are visibly in mitosis across representative fields. The mitotic index is 0.20; active growth is plausible, while phase duration and cell loss still affect interpretation.
  • Checkpoint-arrest culture: After a treatment, metaphase-like cells accumulate while total cell number changes little. Accumulation can reflect delayed progression at a checkpoint rather than faster completion of division.
  • Mixed tumour sample: Different regions show mitotic indices of 0.08, 0.24, and 0.41. The variation shows spatial heterogeneity and warns against representing the entire sample with one field.

Lesson 4 · Cell Division

Meiosis I and II

Why does sexual reproduction require two divisions after one DNA replication?

Required time
110 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C1.3k, C1.4k

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to explain why meiosis uses two divisions after one DNA replication to produce haploid cells and variation.

Success criteria

  • I can distinguish homologous chromosomes from sister chromatids at every meiotic stage.
  • I can trace chromosome sets and DNA amount through meiosis I and II.
  • I can explain independent assortment and crossing over as different sources of variation.

Retrieve

What must be reduced?

Why must a diploid germ-cell lineage reduce chromosome sets before fertilization?

Not saved yet

Pairing

Prophase I brings homologues together

After one S phase, homologous chromosomes pair through synapsis during prophase I. A paired structure contains four chromatids. Non-sister chromatids can exchange corresponding DNA segments through crossing over at chiasmata, producing recombinant chromatids.

Crossing over does not swap whole genes randomly or occur between arbitrary chromosomes; aligned homologous regions are exchanged. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

First division

Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes

At metaphase I, homologous pairs orient at the equator. Each pair can orient independently of other pairs. During anaphase I, homologues move to opposite poles while sister chromatids usually remain joined. The division reduces chromosome sets from diploid to haploid.

Independent assortment describes orientation of homologous pairs, while crossing over changes chromosome segments. Do not treat the mechanisms as synonyms. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Second division

Meiosis II separates sister chromatids

No new DNA replication occurs between meiosis I and II. Chromosomes align individually at metaphase II, and sister chromatids separate during anaphase II. The final products are haploid, but they are not necessarily genetically identical because of assortment, crossing over, and earlier mutation.

Track sets and DNA copies separately: cells are haploid after meiosis I even though chromosomes still have sister chromatids. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Outcome

Meiosis and fertilization form a chromosome-number cycle

Meiosis reduces chromosome sets, and fertilization restores diploidy by combining two haploid gametes. This cycle supports stable species chromosome number across generations while producing new allele combinations. Errors in pairing, recombination, attachment, or segregation can change chromosome content.

A meiotic error is probabilistic and stage-specific; it does not guarantee fertilization or one developmental outcome. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Meiosis chromosome tracker

Inspect three stages of one model homologous pair.

Choose a stage and report homologue, chromatid, set, and variation evidence.

Prophase I

Evidence
Replicated maternal and paternal homologues are synapsed and one chiasma is visible.
Explanation
The tetrad supports pairing and possible recombination between non-sister chromatids.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Draw the pair at each stage and label chromosome sets, chromatids, and exchanged segments.

  • Prophase I: Replicated maternal and paternal homologues are synapsed and one chiasma is visible. The tetrad supports pairing and possible recombination between non-sister chromatids.
  • After meiosis I: Each daughter cell contains one replicated homologue from the original pair. The cells are haploid even though each chromosome still has sister chromatids.
  • After meiosis II: Four cells each contain one unreplicated chromosome from the pair, with two recombinant chromatids among them. Sister separation produced haploid products whose alleles differ because recombination occurred earlier.

Lesson 5 · Cell Division

Spermatogenesis, Oogenesis, and Chromosome Number

How do gamete-production pathways achieve the same chromosome goal differently?

Required time
95 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C1.3k

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to compare spermatogenesis and oogenesis as meiotic pathways with the same chromosome goal and different timing and cell outcomes.

Success criteria

  • I can identify meiotic stages and supporting tissues in each gamete pathway.
  • I can explain equal versus unequal cytokinesis and meiotic pauses.
  • I can compare chromosome outcome without implying that one gamete type is biologically superior.

Retrieve

Same goal, different products

Why can both gamete pathways produce haploid cells even though one commonly yields four small cells and the other one large cell plus polar bodies?

Not saved yet

Spermatogenesis

A continuing lineage produces many small gametes

After puberty, spermatogonial lineages can produce primary spermatocytes that enter meiosis. Meiosis I forms secondary spermatocytes, meiosis II forms spermatids, and later differentiation produces sperm. Cytoplasm is divided relatively evenly, supporting four potential meiotic products from one primary spermatocyte.

Sperm differentiation after meiosis changes shape and function but does not add another chromosome-reduction division. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Oogenesis

A finite lineage includes long meiotic pauses

Primary oocytes begin meiosis before birth and pause in prophase I. Selected cells resume meiosis after puberty. Completion of meiosis I produces a large secondary oocyte and a small polar body. The secondary oocyte typically pauses in metaphase II and completes meiosis II only after fertilization.

Cell name should match meiotic state. An ovulated secondary oocyte has not ordinarily completed meiosis II. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Cytoplasm

Unequal division preserves resources in one cell

Oogenesis allocates most cytoplasm, organelles, and stored molecules to one large cell, while polar bodies receive chromosome sets with little cytoplasm. Spermatogenesis prioritizes many motile cells with less cytoplasm. These are different reproductive strategies, not evidence that one gamete contributes more genetic value.

The zygote normally receives one haploid nuclear set from each gamete even though cytoplasmic contribution differs substantially. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Age and error

Timing changes the context for chromosome segregation

Oocytes may remain paused for years before completing meiosis, while sperm lineages continue dividing and renewing. Age-associated patterns and mutation sources therefore differ between pathways. Population-level probabilities do not determine one gamete or pregnancy outcome.

A nondisjunction pattern requires chromosome evidence; age alone is not a diagnosis or complete cause. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Gametogenesis evidence comparator

Identify pathway and stage from chromosome, cytoplasm, and timing clues.

Choose a case and explain both the shared meiotic goal and the pathway difference.

Four similar products

Evidence
One primary germ cell produces four haploid cells of similar size before motility develops.
Explanation
The pattern fits spermatogenesis after meiosis II and before full sperm differentiation.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Compare starting ploidy, division sequence, product number, cytoplasm, timing, pause, and later differentiation.

  • Four similar products: One primary germ cell produces four haploid cells of similar size before motility develops. The pattern fits spermatogenesis after meiosis II and before full sperm differentiation.
  • One large paused cell: A large haploid cell with replicated chromosomes is paused at metaphase II beside a small polar body. The pattern fits an ovulated secondary oocyte after meiosis I and before completion of meiosis II.
  • Meiosis II completion: Sperm fusion is followed by sister-chromatid separation and extrusion of another polar body. The evidence fits completion of oocyte meiosis II triggered after fertilization begins.

Lesson 6 · Cell Division

Crossing Over, Nondisjunction, and Karyotypes

How can chromosome behaviour generate variation or alter development?

Required time
105 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C1.5k, C1.6k, C1.3s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to interpret crossing over, nondisjunction, and karyotype evidence without treating a chromosome image as a complete diagnosis.

Success criteria

  • I can distinguish recombination from chromosome-number change.
  • I can predict gamete patterns from nondisjunction in meiosis I versus meiosis II.
  • I can read a karyotype for chromosome count and visible structure while naming its resolution limits.

Retrieve

Variation or imbalance?

How can crossing over change allele combinations without changing chromosome number, while nondisjunction can change chromosome number?

Not saved yet

Crossing over

Homologous exchange creates recombinant chromatids

During prophase I, aligned non-sister chromatids can break and rejoin at corresponding regions. Reciprocal exchange can produce new combinations of alleles on the same chromosome without adding or removing entire chromosomes. The frequency of recombination depends partly on distance and chromosome context.

A recombinant chromosome is not automatically abnormal. Recombination is a normal source of variation when exchange is balanced. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Nondisjunction

Segregation failure changes product chromosome content

If homologues fail to separate in meiosis I, all resulting products for that chromosome can have an extra or missing copy. If sister chromatids fail in meiosis II, two products may have typical copy number while one has an extra and one is missing a copy. Fertilization can then produce aneuploid zygotes.

Stage-specific product patterns help infer where segregation failed, but a single surviving cell may not reveal the complete event. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Karyotypes

Chromosome displays summarize large-scale evidence

A karyotype arranges stained metaphase chromosomes by size, centromere position, and banding pattern. It can reveal chromosome number and some large structural changes. It usually cannot show single-base variants, many small deletions, gene expression, receptor function, or every mosaic cell line.

Report what is visible: count, chromosome pair, and large pattern. Do not infer personality, worth, gender, or every health outcome. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Ethics and communication

Chromosome evidence carries privacy and uncertainty

Prenatal, diagnostic, or research chromosome testing involves consent, privacy, possible incidental findings, variable outcomes, and disability perspectives. The same chromosome pattern can be associated with a range of traits. Person-first or identity-first language should follow the preferences of affected communities and individuals.

A classroom karyotype is an instructional model, not clinical interpretation. Decisions require current professional guidance and respect for autonomy. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Nondisjunction and karyotype lab

Compare product sets from three chromosome events.

Choose a pattern and identify the most plausible event plus one uncertainty.

Recombined, balanced

Evidence
Four haploid products each contain one chromosome, and two carry exchanged homologous segments.
Explanation
The count is balanced and the pattern fits normal crossing over followed by segregation.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Draw each division, count tracked copies in every product, and separate event inference from clinical outcome.

  • Recombined, balanced: Four haploid products each contain one chromosome, and two carry exchanged homologous segments. The count is balanced and the pattern fits normal crossing over followed by segregation.
  • Meiosis I nondisjunction: Two products contain two homologues and two contain none for the tracked chromosome. All four products are affected in the characteristic model pattern because homologues failed to separate in meiosis I.
  • Meiosis II nondisjunction: Two products have one copy, one has two sister-derived copies, and one has none. The two typical and two atypical products fit sister-chromatid nondisjunction in one meiosis II cell.

Lesson 7 · Cell Division

Reproductive Strategies and Cell-Division Integration

How do life cycles balance genetic continuity, variation, speed, and survival?

Required time
100 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C1.7k, C1.2s, C1.4s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to compare reproductive life cycles and cell-division strategies by continuity, variation, speed, cost, and environmental context.

Success criteria

  • I can locate mitosis, meiosis, and fertilization in haploid-dominant, diploid-dominant, and alternation-of-generations models.
  • I can compare asexual and sexual reproduction without calling either universally superior.
  • I can evaluate cloning and telomere claims with current, qualified evidence.

Retrieve

Best under which conditions?

Why might a reproductive strategy be advantageous in one environment and costly in another?

Not saved yet

Life cycles

Mitosis and meiosis occur at different ploidy transitions

In a diploid-dominant life cycle, meiosis produces haploid gametes and fertilization restores diploidy. In a haploid-dominant cycle, the zygote undergoes meiosis and much of the organism is haploid. Alternation of generations includes multicellular haploid and diploid stages connected by fertilization and meiosis.

Track ploidy at every arrow. Do not assume meiosis always directly produces gametes in every lineage. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Asexual reproduction

Mitosis can rapidly preserve a successful genotype

Asexual strategies can produce offspring without gamete fusion and may support rapid colonization when conditions are stable. Offspring are genetically similar to the parent except for mutation and other changes. Low recombination can limit the generation of new combinations when environments or pathogens change.

Similarity is not perfect identity, and low variation is not always disadvantageous. Fitness depends on the current environment. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Sexual reproduction

Recombination can create diverse combinations at a cost

Sexual reproduction combines meiosis and fertilization, creating variation through assortment, crossing over, and random gamete union. Costs may include finding mates, specialized structures, slower reproduction, and passing only part of one genome to each offspring. Benefits depend on ecological and evolutionary context.

Avoid framing sexual reproduction as an automatic ladder of progress. Both strategies persist because tradeoffs vary. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Cloning claims

A clone is not a replay of one organism

Cloning by embryo splitting or nuclear transfer can produce a nuclear genome closely related to a donor, but mitochondrial DNA, epigenetic state, prenatal environment, development, and experience can differ. Early claims that one cloned animal’s telomeres proved universal premature aging were oversimplified; cloning outcomes vary and reprogramming is incomplete.

A clone is not genetically or personally identical in every respect, and one animal cannot establish a universal lifespan rule. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Reproductive-strategy evidence board

Compare strategies under changing environmental conditions.

Choose a scenario and identify the conditional advantage without ranking organisms.

Stable environment

Evidence
A well-adapted clonal lineage reproduces rapidly while conditions remain consistent.
Explanation
Rapid asexual reproduction can preserve a successful genotype, though mutation and future change still matter.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Compare mechanism, variation source, time scale, environmental condition, cost, and what the evidence cannot rank.

  • Stable environment: A well-adapted clonal lineage reproduces rapidly while conditions remain consistent. Rapid asexual reproduction can preserve a successful genotype, though mutation and future change still matter.
  • Changing pathogen pressure: A sexually reproducing population contains varied resistance combinations and some survive a new pathogen. Recombination-generated variation can increase the chance that some combinations fit the changed environment.
  • Nuclear-transfer clone: The clone shares most nuclear DNA with a donor but differs in mitochondrial source, epigenetic marks, and developmental environment. The evidence supports close nuclear relatedness, not total genetic, developmental, behavioural, or lifespan identity.

Lesson 8 · Classical Genetics

Mendel, Alleles, and Segregation

How did inheritance ratios reveal rules that could not be seen directly?

Required time
90 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C2.1k

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to explain how Mendel used controlled crosses and ratios to infer segregation of hereditary factors.

Success criteria

  • I can distinguish gene, locus, allele, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, and heterozygous.
  • I can connect meiosis to the law of segregation.
  • I can explain why a useful Mendelian model does not make every trait simple or deterministic.

Retrieve

Invisible factors from visible ratios

How could repeated offspring ratios reveal something about hereditary factors that could not be seen directly?

Not saved yet

Experimental design

Controlled crosses isolate inheritance patterns

Mendel used pea varieties with contrasting traits, controlled pollination, and counted many offspring across generations. True-breeding parental lines produced uniform F1 patterns for selected traits, while F2 generations revealed reappearance of alternatives. Replication and large counts made the ratios informative.

The historical model was powerful because the organisms and traits fit it well. It should not be transferred uncritically to every human or continuous trait. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Alleles

A gene can have alternative sequence forms

A gene occupies a locus, and alleles are alternative versions at that locus. In a diploid organism, two homologues can carry the same allele or different alleles. Homozygous and heterozygous describe genotype at a locus, while phenotype describes an observed trait under particular genetic and environmental conditions.

Dominant means expressed in a heterozygote under the model; it does not mean common, healthy, strong, desirable, or likely to increase. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Segregation

Allele pairs separate when homologues separate

The law of segregation states that two alleles in a diploid individual separate into different gametes. The chromosome mechanism is separation of homologous chromosomes in meiosis I, followed by distribution into haploid products. Fertilization pairs one allele from each contributing gamete source.

A Punnett square represents gamete probabilities and combinations, not a physical movement of letters or a guaranteed family ratio. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Model boundaries

One-gene models are deliberately simplified

Mendelian ratios can be altered by small samples, linkage, incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, penetrance, environmental influence, viability differences, meiotic drive, or scoring error. A model remains useful when its assumptions and limits are explicit.

Select examples with validated inheritance. Avoid textbook claims that tongue rolling, attached earlobes, eye colour, or many other complex human traits are single-gene binaries. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Mendelian ratio interpreter

Compare three offspring samples generated from the same theoretical cross.

Choose a sample and distinguish expected probability from observed count.

Large sample

Evidence
A monohybrid F2 sample of 1,200 offspring is close to a 3:1 phenotype ratio.
Explanation
The large sample is consistent with the simple dominance and segregation model, while consistency is not proof that no alternative exists.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

For each sample, state theoretical probability, observed count, sample size, variation, and next evidence.

  • Large sample: A monohybrid F2 sample of 1,200 offspring is close to a 3:1 phenotype ratio. The large sample is consistent with the simple dominance and segregation model, while consistency is not proof that no alternative exists.
  • Small sample: A family-sized sample of four offspring shows four dominant phenotypes. The outcome is possible under a 3:1 probability and does not show that segregation failed.
  • Consistent departure: Repeated large crosses show a stable ratio far from the Mendelian prediction. The pattern justifies testing linkage, viability, scoring, penetrance, or another model assumption.

Lesson 9 · Classical Genetics

Monohybrid Crosses

How can genotype probability predict phenotype without guaranteeing an outcome?

Required time
100 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C2.1k, C2.2k

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to construct and interpret monohybrid crosses as probability models rather than guarantees.

Success criteria

  • I can derive gamete alleles from parental genotypes.
  • I can calculate genotype and phenotype probabilities for a validated one-locus model.
  • I can state assumptions, separate probability from prediction for one child, and check my work.

Retrieve

Gametes first

Why should a Punnett-square solution begin by deriving possible gametes instead of placing parental genotypes directly in every box?

Not saved yet

Model setup

Define the inheritance model before calculating

A monohybrid cross follows one locus. State allele symbols, dominance relation, parental genotypes, and the phenotype-genotype link. Use uppercase and lowercase only as labels; letters do not make one allele stronger. The example must have evidence for the assumed inheritance pattern.

A correct grid built on an incorrect model still produces a misleading answer. Record assumptions before arithmetic. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Gamete derivation

Each gamete receives one allele copy

A heterozygous diploid Aa produces A-bearing and a-bearing gametes under the simple segregation model, commonly at equal probability. A homozygous AA parent produces only A-bearing gametes for the locus. List gamete types and probabilities along the grid axes.

The grid combines gametes; it does not show meiosis itself. Link the probabilities back to homologue separation. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Combination

Boxes represent equally likely unions only under stated assumptions

For Aa × Aa, the four combinations are AA, Aa, Aa, and aa, giving genotype probabilities 1/4, 1/2, and 1/4. With complete dominance, phenotype probabilities are 3/4 dominant and 1/4 recessive. Repeated boxes represent probability weight, not different genotypes.

Check that genotype probabilities sum to 1 and that phenotype categories include every genotype exactly once. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Interpretation

Each reproductive event is a new probability trial

A 1/4 probability does not mean every fourth child must have the phenotype or that previous outcomes change the next probability under the model. Small families can show many ratios. Probability supports counselling and prediction only when the inheritance model, parent genotypes, penetrance, and evidence are appropriate.

Avoid deterministic wording and remember that real human traits can involve multiple genes, environment, and incomplete information. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Monohybrid probability lab

Compare crosses with different parental genotype evidence.

Choose a cross and calculate the correct probability statement.

aa × aa

Evidence
Both parents produce only a-bearing gametes in the model.
Explanation
All offspring are predicted aa at this locus, assuming parent genotypes and model are correct.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Write parental genotypes, gamete probabilities, combinations, totals, phenotype mapping, and assumptions.

  • aa × aa: Both parents produce only a-bearing gametes in the model. All offspring are predicted aa at this locus, assuming parent genotypes and model are correct.
  • aa × Aa: One parent produces only a gametes and the other produces A or a gametes equally. Offspring genotype probabilities are 1/2 Aa and 1/2 aa.
  • Aa × Aa: Both parents produce A and a gametes with equal probability. Offspring genotype probabilities are 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, and 1/4 aa.

Lesson 10 · Classical Genetics

Probability, Test Crosses, and Sampling Variation

Why do observed ratios approach predictions without matching them exactly?

Required time
95 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C2.2k, C2.1s, C2.2s, C2.3s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to use multiplication, addition, test crosses, and sampling evidence to evaluate inheritance probabilities.

Success criteria

  • I can choose multiplication for joint independent events and addition for mutually exclusive routes.
  • I can use a test cross to update an unknown genotype explanation.
  • I can compare observed and expected counts without assuming small deviations disprove a model.

Retrieve

And or either?

When should probabilities be multiplied, and when should they be added in a genetics problem?

Not saved yet

Probability rules

Multiplication and addition answer different questions

For independent events that must both occur, multiply probabilities. For mutually exclusive routes that lead to the same outcome, add their probabilities. A heterozygote can arise through A from one parent and a from the other or the reverse route; the two route probabilities are added.

Write the event statement before the operation. Arithmetic without event definitions is difficult to audit. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Test cross

A recessive partner exposes an unknown allele contribution

An organism with a dominant phenotype may be AA or Aa in a complete-dominance model. Crossing with aa makes the predictions differ: AA × aa produces all Aa, while Aa × aa predicts half Aa and half aa. Offspring evidence changes confidence in the alternatives.

All dominant offspring in a small sample do not prove AA because the heterozygous model can produce that pattern by chance. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Sampling variation

Observed counts fluctuate around probability

Expected counts equal probability multiplied by sample size, but random segregation and fertilization create variation. Larger samples usually show smaller proportional deviations. Repeated departures can also reflect linkage, viability, scoring, non-random sampling, or an incorrect inheritance model.

Report observed and expected counts, sample size, direction and magnitude of departure, and whether a formal goodness-of-fit test is appropriate. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Model revision

Evidence updates rather than instantly proves

A test-cross result can make one genotype more plausible, but confidence depends on sample size, parentage, penetrance, scoring, and model validity. Scientific reasoning asks how likely the data are under each explanation and what next observation would discriminate.

Use probabilistic language such as “supports,” “is consistent with,” and “is less likely,” not “proves” when alternatives remain. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Test-cross evidence updater

Compare increasing samples from an unknown dominant-phenotype parent crossed with aa.

Choose a sample and identify the supported genotype without claiming certainty beyond the data.

Four dominant offspring

Evidence
All four offspring have the dominant phenotype.
Explanation
AA is compatible, but Aa remains possible because four dominant outcomes can occur by chance.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

For each sample, calculate prediction under AA and Aa, compare observed likelihood, and name assumptions.

  • Four dominant offspring: All four offspring have the dominant phenotype. AA is compatible, but Aa remains possible because four dominant outcomes can occur by chance.
  • Recessive offspring present: Among eight offspring, three have the recessive phenotype. Under the simple model, the unknown parent must have contributed a, supporting heterozygous Aa.
  • Large near-half sample: Among 200 offspring, 96 are recessive and 104 dominant. The pattern closely fits the Aa × aa expectation and strongly supports heterozygosity under the model.

Lesson 11 · Classical Genetics

Incomplete Dominance, Codominance, and Multiple Alleles

What changes when alleles do not follow a simple dominant-recessive pattern?

Required time
100 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C2.2k, C2.4k

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to model incomplete dominance, codominance, and multiple alleles without confusing phenotype expression with allele frequency or value.

Success criteria

  • I can distinguish complete dominance, incomplete dominance, and codominance by heterozygote evidence.
  • I can solve a multiple-allele problem while remembering that one individual carries at most two alleles at an autosomal locus.
  • I can select a model from evidence rather than forcing every trait into dominant-recessive notation.

Retrieve

Look at the heterozygote

What phenotype evidence would distinguish incomplete dominance from codominance?

Not saved yet

Incomplete dominance

The heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype

In incomplete dominance, neither allele produces the same heterozygote phenotype as either homozygote under the measured conditions. A red-flowered and white-flowered model can produce pink heterozygotes. The alleles themselves do not blend permanently; segregation can recover both homozygous phenotypes.

An F2 phenotype ratio can match 1:2:1 because each genotype has a distinguishable phenotype. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Codominance

Both allele products are detectably expressed

In codominance, heterozygotes show products associated with both alleles, as in AB blood-group antigen expression. Codominance does not mean every cell or molecule is half one and half another; it means both allele effects are detected in the defined phenotype.

Select the model from molecular or phenotype evidence, not from whether one trait sounds visually stronger. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Multiple alleles

Populations can contain more alleles than an individual

A locus can have several allele forms in a population. The ABO blood-group model includes IA, IB, and i, while a diploid individual ordinarily carries two. IA and IB are codominant to each other and each is dominant to i in the simplified antigen model.

Allele hierarchy must be stated explicitly. Blood type alone may not uniquely determine genotype for A or B phenotypes. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Model choice

Notation should preserve the biology

Superscripts or distinct symbols reduce the misleading implication that one allele is inherently superior. Before calculating, define allele products, heterozygote phenotype, genotype-phenotype map, and population scope. Environment and measurement method can still affect phenotype.

These models explain selected loci; they should not be generalized to complex human characteristics or social categories. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Heterozygote model lab

Compare three loci with different heterozygote evidence.

Choose a locus and identify the appropriate expression model.

Intermediate pigment

Evidence
The heterozygote has a quantitatively intermediate pigment concentration between two homozygotes.
Explanation
The evidence fits incomplete dominance for the measured pigment phenotype.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Define the phenotype measurement, compare three genotypes, choose the model, and state whether another measurement could change the classification.

  • Intermediate pigment: The heterozygote has a quantitatively intermediate pigment concentration between two homozygotes. The evidence fits incomplete dominance for the measured pigment phenotype.
  • Both antigens: A heterozygote displays two distinct cell-surface antigens associated with different alleles. Simultaneous detection of both products fits codominance.
  • One phenotype class: A heterozygote and one homozygote share the scored phenotype, while molecular amounts differ. The scored phenotype fits complete dominance, though molecular evidence can reveal additional quantitative variation.

Lesson 12 · Classical Genetics

Dihybrid Crosses and Independent Assortment

How do two gene pairs combine to create a larger probability space?

Required time
115 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C2.1k, C2.2k

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to solve dihybrid probability problems and explain when independent assortment is a valid assumption.

Success criteria

  • I can derive gametes for two unlinked loci using meiosis or probability.
  • I can calculate joint genotype or phenotype probabilities without relying only on a 16-box grid.
  • I can explain why linkage or other model violations change expected ratios.

Retrieve

Two loci, one gamete

A parent is AaBb. What must be true for AB, Ab, aB, and ab gametes to be equally likely?

Not saved yet

Independent assortment

Homologous pairs orient independently in meiosis I

When loci are on different chromosome pairs—or effectively unlinked—the orientation of one homologous pair does not determine another. An AaBb parent then produces AB, Ab, aB, and ab gametes with equal probability under the simple model.

Independent assortment is a chromosome-behaviour assumption, not a statement that every gene in a genome is independent. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Branch method

Multiply locus probabilities for joint outcomes

A dihybrid cross can be decomposed into two monohybrid crosses when loci assort independently. For AaBb × AaBb, the probability of aa is 1/4 and bb is 1/4, so aabb is 1/16. The method reduces grid errors and makes assumptions visible.

Use addition when several mutually exclusive genotype routes produce the same requested phenotype. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Grid method

A 4-by-4 grid represents sixteen gamete unions

Listing four gametes from each heterozygous parent yields sixteen equally weighted boxes under the model. With complete dominance at both loci, phenotype classes can form a 9:3:3:1 ratio. That ratio depends on segregation, independent assortment, dominance, equal viability, and adequate sample size.

Do not memorize 9:3:3:1 without connecting it to gamete probabilities and assumptions. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Departures

Linkage and sampling change observed patterns

Genes on the same chromosome can be inherited together more often than predicted by independence, especially when close. Recombination can still produce non-parental combinations. Small samples fluctuate, and viability or scoring can also alter ratios.

A ratio departure is evidence to investigate, not automatic proof of linkage. Compare reciprocal classes, recombination, sample size, and alternative explanations. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Dihybrid probability builder

Compare independent and linked-looking offspring patterns.

Choose a case and identify the calculation and model test.

Near 9:3:3:1

Evidence
A large AaBb × AaBb cross approximates four phenotype classes in a 9:3:3:1 pattern.
Explanation
The data are consistent with independent assortment and complete dominance under the model.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Calculate expected counts, compare class symmetry and sample size, and test linkage against alternatives.

  • Near 9:3:3:1: A large AaBb × AaBb cross approximates four phenotype classes in a 9:3:3:1 pattern. The data are consistent with independent assortment and complete dominance under the model.
  • Parental combinations in excess: A test cross produces far more AB and ab offspring than Ab and aB offspring. The excess parental combinations supports linkage with recombination producing the smaller classes.
  • Small uneven sample: Sixteen offspring show 11, 1, 3, and 1 across four phenotype classes. The sample is too small for the deviation alone to identify linkage; repeated larger evidence is needed.

Lesson 13 · Classical Genetics

Sex Linkage and Pedigree Evidence

How can family patterns distinguish autosomal and sex-linked inheritance?

Required time
110 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C2.5k, C2.3s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to interpret sex-linked inheritance and pedigrees as evidence with uncertainty, not as automatic genotype labels.

Success criteria

  • I can model X-linked inheritance using chromosome-aware notation.
  • I can distinguish autosomal, X-linked, Y-linked, and mitochondrial clues without relying on one shortcut.
  • I can annotate a pedigree with possible genotypes and state why family data may remain ambiguous.

Retrieve

One X changes probability

Why can an X-linked recessive allele have different expression probabilities in people with one X chromosome versus two?

Not saved yet

Chromosome context

Sex-linked loci travel with sex chromosomes

An X-linked locus is located on the X chromosome. A person with one X has one allele copy at many X-linked loci, while a person with two X chromosomes can carry two. Y-linked loci pass through Y-chromosome inheritance. Chromosomal and developmental variation means classroom categories are simplified.

Use karyotype and inheritance context stated in the fictional case. Do not infer gender identity from pedigree symbols or chromosome assumptions. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

X-linked model

Recessive expression depends on allele context

In a simplified X-linked recessive model, a person with one X carrying the allele can express the phenotype because no second allele at the locus is present. A heterozygous person with two X chromosomes may be described as a carrier, though X-inactivation, penetrance, and phenotype definition can affect expression.

Use superscript notation and include chromosome contribution from each gamete source. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Pedigree clues

Patterns support alternatives rather than one magic rule

X-linked recessive patterns may show more affected people with one X and no father-to-son transmission under the simplified model. Autosomal patterns can affect sexes similarly, while mitochondrial inheritance follows the egg lineage. Small pedigrees, missing people, uncertain parentage, variable penetrance, and new mutation can obscure patterns.

No single affected individual establishes the inheritance mode. Compare the whole pedigree and list genotypes as known, possible, or excluded. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Ethics

Family genetic evidence is private and relational

A result can reveal information about biological relatives who did not choose testing. Pedigree analysis can also intersect with adoption, donor conception, misattributed parentage, and cultural definitions of family. Classroom work must use fictional pedigrees and avoid collecting real family health histories.

Clinical interpretation requires consent, counselling, validated testing, and respectful communication of uncertainty. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Pedigree evidence analyzer

Compare three fictional transmission patterns.

Choose a pedigree summary and identify the best-supported model plus an ambiguity.

No father-to-son pattern

Evidence
Affected people with one X occur across generations; affected fathers have no affected sons through paternal X transmission.
Explanation
The pattern supports an X-linked model, while small sample and penetrance still require caution.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Mark observed phenotype, chromosome source, possible genotypes, excluded routes, missing data, and privacy limits.

  • No father-to-son pattern: Affected people with one X occur across generations; affected fathers have no affected sons through paternal X transmission. The pattern supports an X-linked model, while small sample and penetrance still require caution.
  • All sexes and father-to-son: Affected people of several sexes occur, including repeated father-to-son transmission. The father-to-son evidence argues against X linkage and supports an autosomal alternative under the model.
  • Egg-line transmission: Affected mothers can transmit the trait to children, while affected fathers do not transmit it. The direction supports mitochondrial inheritance, though heteroplasmy and variable expression can change the phenotype pattern.

Lesson 14 · Classical Genetics

Gene Linkage, Crossing Over, and Chromosome Maps

How can recombination frequency become a map of relative gene position?

Required time
115 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C2.3k, C2.3s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to use recombination frequency as evidence for gene linkage and relative chromosome-map distance.

Success criteria

  • I can identify parental and recombinant classes in a test cross.
  • I can calculate recombination frequency and map units with a clear denominator.
  • I can explain why two-point data underestimate long distances and do not uniquely establish gene order.

Retrieve

A map from offspring

How can offspring phenotype counts provide evidence about the distance between genes on a chromosome?

Not saved yet

Linkage

Genes on one chromosome can travel together

Loci on the same chromosome are linked, but crossing over can create recombinant chromatids. Close loci have fewer opportunities for a crossover between them than loci farther apart. In a test cross, offspring classes can reveal gamete types from the heterozygous parent.

The most frequent classes are often parental and smaller reciprocal classes recombinant, assuming viability and scoring do not bias counts. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Calculation

Recombination frequency estimates relative distance

Recombination frequency equals recombinant offspring divided by total offspring, multiplied by 100 percent. One percent recombination is defined as approximately one map unit or centimorgan. Show both reciprocal recombinant classes and use the full sample denominator.

A map unit is a statistical distance, not an exact physical base-pair length that is constant across species or chromosome regions. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Limits

Observed recombination cannot exceed fifty percent

Multiple crossovers can restore a parental arrangement and go undetected in a two-point cross. Widely separated loci therefore approach 50 percent recombination and can appear unlinked. Recombination rates also vary by sex, species, chromosome region, and biological context.

Two-point frequency estimates order poorly over long intervals. Three-point crosses or molecular markers provide stronger mapping evidence. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Gene order

Three loci require comparison of crossover classes

In a three-point test cross, largest classes are often parental and smallest classes double crossovers. Comparing allele arrangement between these classes can identify the middle gene. Distances are estimated for adjacent intervals and checked against observed double-crossovers.

Gene order is an inference from class patterns and assumptions. Label synthetic data and test for viability or scoring effects before concluding. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Chromosome mapping lab

Analyze three synthetic test-cross datasets.

Choose a dataset and calculate the strongest map claim.

Close loci

Evidence
A test cross has 92 recombinant offspring among 1,000 total.
Explanation
The estimated distance is 9.2 map units, assuming the recombinant classes are correctly identified and similarly viable.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

List every class, classify reciprocal pairs, calculate frequencies, infer order, and state undetected-crossover limits.

  • Close loci: A test cross has 92 recombinant offspring among 1,000 total. The estimated distance is 9.2 map units, assuming the recombinant classes are correctly identified and similarly viable.
  • Near fifty percent: A two-point cross has 486 recombinants among 1,000 offspring. The loci behave as effectively unlinked in this dataset; they may be on different chromosomes or far apart on one chromosome.
  • Double-crossover clue: Two very small reciprocal classes differ from parental classes only at locus M. The pattern supports M as the middle locus, with adjacent interval calculations needed for the map.

Lesson 15 · Classical Genetics

Polygenic Traits, Environment, and Genetic Decisions

How should models and evidence be used when traits have many genetic and environmental influences?

Required time
95 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C2.4k, C2.1sts, C2.1s, C2.2s, C2.4s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to explain polygenic and environmentally influenced traits and evaluate genetic decisions without simplistic human-trait claims.

Success criteria

  • I can distinguish single-locus, polygenic, multifactorial, penetrance, and expressivity models.
  • I can interpret a continuous distribution without assigning one gene to each category.
  • I can evaluate genetic information through evidence, uncertainty, privacy, equity, and informed consent.

Retrieve

Beyond two boxes

Why do height, many health risks, and numerous physiological measurements form continuous distributions rather than simple dominant-recessive groups?

Not saved yet

Polygenic inheritance

Many loci can contribute small effects

A polygenic trait is influenced by variants at multiple loci. Additive models can produce many genotype combinations and a range of phenotypes, but real interactions may be non-additive. No single “tall gene,” “intelligence gene,” or “athletic gene” explains a complex human outcome.

A distribution can shift with allele frequencies while retaining substantial overlap. Group averages do not identify an individual genotype or ability. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Environment and development

Phenotype emerges through interaction

Nutrition, health, learning, stress, physical environment, social conditions, random developmental events, and measurement context can influence phenotype. Gene-environment interaction means a genetic effect can differ across environments; it does not mean genes and environment contribute separable fixed percentages to one person.

Heritability describes variation in a studied population and environment, not immutability, personal destiny, or the fraction of an individual caused by genes. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Penetrance and expressivity

The same variant may not produce one identical phenotype

Penetrance describes the proportion of people with a genotype who show a defined phenotype. Expressivity describes variation in degree or form among those who show it. Modifier genes, environment, age, sex-related biology, mosaicism, and measurement definitions can contribute.

A risk variant changes probability under defined evidence; it does not guarantee disease or absence of disease. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Genetic decisions

Information can help and harm

Genetic testing can support diagnosis, screening, reproductive planning, treatment selection, or research, while raising questions about validity, uncertain findings, privacy, family implications, discrimination, access, ancestry databases, data governance, and Indigenous data sovereignty. Benefits and harms depend on purpose and context.

A responsible brief asks whether the test is analytically valid, clinically meaningful, actionable, consented to, equitably accessible, and governed by affected people. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Complex-trait evidence evaluator

Compare three genetic claims with different evidence quality.

Choose a claim and replace deterministic wording with a valid interpretation.

Risk score

Evidence
A score trained in one population is associated with a modest shift in disease probability and performs less well in another population.
Explanation
The score is population- and model-dependent; it changes probability rather than diagnosing an individual and requires validation across groups.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Identify population, phenotype definition, effect size, validation, overlap, uncertainty, privacy, and actionability.

  • Risk score: A score trained in one population is associated with a modest shift in disease probability and performs less well in another population. The score is population- and model-dependent; it changes probability rather than diagnosing an individual and requires validation across groups.
  • Heritability claim: A study reports high heritability for a trait in one well-nourished population. The statistic describes variation in that context and does not show that environment is unimportant or change is impossible.
  • Direct-to-consumer result: A report labels one common variant as determining a complex performance trait. The single-variant deterministic claim is not supported for a multifactorial trait and may omit validity, ancestry, environment, and uncertainty.

Lesson 16 · Molecular Genetics

DNA Evidence, History, and Structure

How did converging evidence support the double-helix model?

Required time
85 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C3.1k, C3.2k

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to explain how converging evidence—including Rosalind Franklin’s diffraction work—supported the DNA double-helix model.

Success criteria

  • I can describe nucleotide structure, antiparallel strands, complementary pairing, and major grooves at the course level.
  • I can connect transformation, base-ratio, and diffraction evidence to model constraints.
  • I can represent DNA history as collaborative and evidence-based rather than a single-person discovery story.

Retrieve

A model constrained by evidence

What observations would a DNA model need to explain besides simply looking like a helix?

Not saved yet

Information molecule

Evidence identified DNA as hereditary material

Transformation experiments showed that heritable information could move between bacterial cells. Work by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty supported DNA as the transforming principle, and Hershey-Chase bacteriophage evidence further distinguished DNA from protein in that system. These studies did not by themselves reveal molecular structure.

History is cumulative: each experiment answered a different question with particular organisms, methods, and limits. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Chemical constraints

Nucleotides form directional polymers

Each DNA nucleotide includes deoxyribose, phosphate, and a nitrogenous base. Phosphodiester bonds create a sugar-phosphate backbone with 5-prime to 3-prime direction. Chargaff’s base measurements showed approximate A=T and G=C relationships in double-stranded DNA while base composition varies among species.

Base ratios constrain pairing but do not alone prove a helix or explain strand orientation. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Diffraction evidence

Franklin and Wilkins produced structural constraints

Rosalind Franklin’s careful X-ray diffraction work, including the image known as Photo 51 produced with Raymond Gosling, provided evidence of helical regularity, dimensions, and phosphate placement. Maurice Wilkins also contributed diffraction work. Data access and credit occurred in an unequal historical context that should be represented accurately.

Diffraction patterns require mathematical and physical interpretation; they are evidence, not a direct photograph of a DNA molecule. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Double-helix model

Complementary antiparallel strands explain copying

Watson and Crick assembled a model consistent with chemical and diffraction constraints: two antiparallel strands, sugar-phosphate backbones outward, and complementary base pairs inward. A-T and G-C pairing provides consistent width and a mechanism for templated copying. Later evidence refined DNA forms, dynamics, protein interactions, and chromatin organization.

Scientific models are credited through the evidence network, not only the final published structure. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

DNA model constraint lab

Test three candidate models against historical evidence.

Choose a candidate and identify which evidence it satisfies or violates.

Phosphates inside

Evidence
A model places negatively charged phosphate groups tightly in the helix centre and does not fit measured width.
Explanation
The model conflicts with chemical and diffraction constraints and would create unfavorable charge crowding.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

List each candidate’s strand direction, backbone location, pairing, width, evidence fit, and testable prediction.

  • Phosphates inside: A model places negatively charged phosphate groups tightly in the helix centre and does not fit measured width. The model conflicts with chemical and diffraction constraints and would create unfavorable charge crowding.
  • Parallel random bases: Two strands run in the same direction and bases pair without consistent complementarity. The model fails base-ratio and geometry constraints and offers a weak templating mechanism.
  • Antiparallel complement: Two outward backbones surround complementary base pairs and fit the repeating diffraction dimensions. The model integrates chemical, Chargaff, and diffraction evidence and predicts template-based replication.
