Lesson 17 · Molecular Genetics

DNA Replication

How does molecular structure make accurate copying possible?

Required time
100 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C3.2k, C3.2s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to explain semiconservative DNA replication as coordinated unwinding, priming, synthesis, proofreading, and joining.

Success criteria

  • I can identify the roles of helicase, single-strand-binding proteins, primase, DNA polymerase, and ligase.
  • I can explain leading and lagging synthesis from antiparallel templates.
  • I can use evidence to distinguish replication error, repair, and inherited mutation.

Retrieve

One direction on opposite templates

If DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to a 3-prime end, why must the two new strands be synthesized differently at a replication fork?

Not saved yet

Semiconservative model

Each daughter molecule keeps one parental strand

Replication begins at origins and proceeds through forks. Helicase separates base pairs, topological strain is managed, and single-strand-binding proteins stabilize exposed templates. Each parental strand guides a complementary new strand, producing daughter molecules with one old and one new strand.

Semiconservative replication was tested with isotope-density evidence; complementarity alone suggested but did not prove the model. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Initiation

Polymerase requires a primer and a template

Primase synthesizes short RNA primers that provide a free 3-prime hydroxyl. DNA polymerases extend from primers by adding complementary deoxyribonucleotides in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction. Base-pair geometry and enzyme active sites support fidelity.

Polymerase does not begin a strand from nothing and does not read the template in the same direction as synthesis. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Two strands

Leading and lagging synthesis solve antiparallel geometry

The leading strand can be synthesized continuously toward the moving fork on one template. The lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously away from the fork as Okazaki fragments. Primers are removed or replaced, and DNA ligase seals remaining backbone gaps.

Both strands are synthesized 5-prime to 3-prime. The labels describe relation to fork movement, not different chemical direction. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Fidelity

Proofreading and repair reduce—but do not eliminate—errors

Polymerase proofreading can remove some mismatched nucleotides, and additional repair systems inspect DNA. An unrepaired change becomes a mutation after it is fixed in a DNA molecule and propagated. Somatic and germ-line contexts differ in whether a variant can pass to offspring.

A DNA change can be neutral, harmful, or beneficial depending on location, cell, environment, and effect; mutation is not synonymous with disease. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Replication sequence model

Diagnose three stalled replication forks.

Choose a case and connect the missing activity to the observed molecular evidence.

Primase absent

Evidence
Templates are open, but no new DNA begins at expected initiation sites.
Explanation
Without primers, DNA polymerase lacks a starting 3-prime end despite available template.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Arrange enzyme, substrate, direction, product, and predicted failure evidence for each step.

  • Primase absent: Templates are open, but no new DNA begins at expected initiation sites. Without primers, DNA polymerase lacks a starting 3-prime end despite available template.
  • Ligase absent: Lagging-strand DNA contains many completed fragments separated by backbone nicks. Synthesis occurred, but ligase-dependent sealing of fragment junctions is incomplete.
  • Proofreading reduced: Replication completes, but mismatched-base frequency rises across daughter molecules. Reduced proofreading increases replication errors while not implying that every mismatch persists or changes phenotype.

Lesson 18 · Molecular Genetics

Transcription

How is a DNA sequence converted into a portable RNA message?

Required time
100 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C3.3k, C3.2s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to explain transcription as regulated RNA synthesis from one DNA template strand.

Success criteria

  • I can identify promoter, template strand, coding strand, RNA polymerase, transcript, and termination.
  • I can write an RNA sequence with correct complementarity and 5-prime/3-prime direction.
  • I can distinguish transcription, RNA processing, and translation in location and product.

Retrieve

One gene, one template strand

Why is only one DNA strand used as the template for a particular transcript, even though both strands contain nucleotide sequences?

Not saved yet

Initiation

Promoters orient RNA synthesis

Transcription begins when regulatory proteins and RNA polymerase assemble at a promoter. Promoter orientation determines which DNA strand is the template and where transcription starts. Gene regulation changes when, where, and how much RNA is produced; not every gene is transcribed in every cell.

A promoter is a DNA regulatory region, not part of the amino-acid sequence, and different genes use different regulatory contexts. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Elongation

RNA grows 5-prime to 3-prime

RNA polymerase reads the DNA template 3-prime to 5-prime and adds complementary ribonucleotides to the RNA 3-prime end. RNA uses uracil instead of thymine. The RNA sequence resembles the coding DNA strand except U replaces T, when both are written 5-prime to 3-prime.

Always label strand direction. Complementing a coding strand directly without considering orientation is a common error. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Termination and processing

A primary transcript can be modified

Termination signals end transcription. In eukaryotes, a primary pre-mRNA is processed through 5-prime capping, poly-A addition, and splicing that removes introns and joins exons. Alternative splicing can produce different mature RNAs from one gene under regulated conditions.

Introns are not simply useless DNA, and one gene does not always equal one protein product. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Regulation and evidence

RNA abundance is a snapshot of expression

Measuring RNA can reveal which genes are transcribed in a sample, but RNA abundance also reflects degradation, cell composition, timing, and method. It does not automatically establish protein amount or activity because translation and protein turnover add later regulation.

A cell-expression claim should name tissue, condition, time, reference genes, and measurement uncertainty. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Transcription model

Compare sequence and expression evidence from three gene states.

Choose a case and identify the transcription or processing step.

Promoter inaccessible

Evidence
The gene’s DNA sequence is present, but RNA polymerase occupancy and transcript abundance are low.
Explanation
The evidence supports reduced transcription initiation rather than deletion of the gene.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Label promoter, template, RNA direction, exons, introns, measured product, and later regulatory alternatives.

  • Promoter inaccessible: The gene’s DNA sequence is present, but RNA polymerase occupancy and transcript abundance are low. The evidence supports reduced transcription initiation rather than deletion of the gene.
  • Splice variant: Two mature RNAs share exons 1 and 3, while only one includes exon 2. Alternative splicing produced distinct mature transcripts from the same gene region.
  • RNA-protein mismatch: mRNA abundance rises, but protein abundance remains low. Transcription increased, while translation efficiency or protein degradation may limit protein accumulation.

Lesson 19 · Molecular Genetics

Translation and Gene Expression

How does a nucleotide message become an amino-acid sequence?

Required time
110 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C3.3k, C3.2s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to explain translation as codon-directed assembly and folding of a polypeptide.

Success criteria

  • I can distinguish mRNA codon, tRNA anticodon, amino acid, ribosome site, and polypeptide.
  • I can translate a sequence from the correct start, direction, and reading frame.
  • I can explain why amino-acid sequence influences—but does not alone determine—final protein function.

Retrieve

Three bases at a time

Why does shifting the reading frame by one nucleotide change many downstream codons?

Not saved yet

Genetic code

Codons connect nucleotide sequence to amino acids

The genetic code uses three-nucleotide mRNA codons. AUG commonly establishes a start codon and specifies methionine, while UAA, UAG, and UGA serve as stop signals in the standard code. The code is redundant because several codons can specify the same amino acid, but it is not ambiguous within the standard table.

Read the mRNA 5-prime to 3-prime from the established start. A DNA sequence must first be identified as template or coding and converted correctly. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

tRNA and ribosome

Adaptor molecules align amino acids with codons

Each charged tRNA carries an amino acid and presents an anticodon that base-pairs antiparallel with a codon. The ribosome positions tRNAs in A, P, and E sites and catalyzes peptide-bond formation through ribosomal RNA activity. The mRNA moves through the ribosome one codon at a time.

tRNA does not carry a DNA gene, and a ribosome does not decide which amino acid feels appropriate; molecular recognition drives the sequence. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Initiation to termination

Translation has ordered stages

Initiation assembles the small ribosomal subunit, mRNA, initiator tRNA, and large subunit at the start region. Elongation cycles add amino acids and move the ribosome. At a stop codon, release factors—not a stop tRNA—promote polypeptide release and complex disassembly.

A premature stop can shorten a polypeptide, but cellular consequences depend on transcript surveillance and protein context. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Protein fate

Sequence enters a larger folding and regulation system

A polypeptide can fold, combine with other subunits, be cleaved, acquire chemical modifications, and move to a specific cellular location. Chaperones and cellular conditions influence folding. Protein function depends on three-dimensional structure, interactions, amount, location, and timing.

A codon change may be synonymous, alter an amino acid, create a stop, affect splicing, or have no measurable phenotype. Sequence consequence is context-dependent. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Translation codon lab

Translate and compare three mRNA changes.

Choose a sequence change and identify its immediate molecular consequence.

Synonymous codon

Evidence
A codon changes from GAA to GAG in the same reading frame; both specify glutamate.
Explanation
The amino-acid sequence is unchanged, though RNA-level effects remain possible.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Write mRNA direction, start position, codon groups, anticodon pairing, amino-acid sequence, and bounded protein prediction.

  • Synonymous codon: A codon changes from GAA to GAG in the same reading frame; both specify glutamate. The amino-acid sequence is unchanged, though RNA-level effects remain possible.
  • Amino-acid substitution: A coding-region codon changes so a different amino acid enters the polypeptide. The immediate effect is a missense substitution; protein effect depends on position, chemistry, and structure.
  • Reading-frame shift: One nucleotide is inserted near the start of a coding sequence without a compensating deletion. Downstream codon grouping changes and a premature stop may appear, often producing a larger sequence consequence.

Lesson 20 · Molecular Genetics

Mutations, Variation, and Cancer Evidence

When does a DNA change have no effect, alter a trait, or contribute to disease?

Required time
105 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C3.6k, C3.1s, C3.3s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to classify mutations, predict molecular consequences, and evaluate cancer evidence without treating mutation as automatically harmful.

Success criteria

  • I can distinguish substitution, insertion, deletion, frameshift, chromosomal, somatic, and germ-line changes.
  • I can trace a DNA change through RNA, protein, cell, and organism evidence.
  • I can compare driver, passenger, repair, environment, and selection explanations in cancer data.

Retrieve

Change is not consequence

Why can the same category of DNA change have very different effects depending on its location and cellular context?

Not saved yet

Mutation types

DNA changes vary in scale and location

A substitution changes one base pair; an insertion or deletion adds or removes sequence; non-multiple-of-three coding indels can shift a reading frame. Larger changes include duplications, inversions, translocations, copy-number changes, and chromosome-number differences. Mutations can arise from replication error, damage, repair, or mobile elements.

Classification describes the DNA event, not whether the outcome is beneficial, neutral, or harmful. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Consequence pathway

Most DNA change effects are filtered through context

A change outside coding sequence can affect regulation, splicing, chromosome organization, or have no measurable effect. Coding changes can be synonymous, missense, nonsense, or frameshifting. Protein effect depends on domain, chemistry, dosage, expression, interactions, and compensation.

Trace evidence level by level instead of jumping from DNA variant directly to a person’s phenotype. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Lineage

Somatic and germ-line mutations have different inheritance routes

A somatic mutation arises in a body-cell lineage and can be passed to its mitotic descendants but ordinarily not to offspring. A germ-line mutation can enter a gamete lineage and be inherited. Mosaicism occurs when cell populations within one organism differ genetically.

Tissue sample, variant fraction, and developmental timing help infer lineage; one blood sample may not represent every tissue. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Cancer evidence

Cancer can emerge through mutation and selection

Cancer often involves accumulated regulatory changes affecting proliferation, repair, death, genome stability, immune interaction, metabolism, and tissue invasion. Some variants drive growth; many passengers accompany expansion. Environmental exposures can change mutation rates or selection, while inherited variants can alter risk.

A tumour sequence is not a complete cause or prognosis. Interpretation needs matched tissue, function, frequency, tumour context, treatment evidence, and clinical expertise. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Mutation consequence lab

Compare three sequence changes with different evidence paths.

Choose a case and stop the claim at the strongest supported level.

Deep intronic variant

Evidence
A base substitution occurs far from known splice and regulatory regions; RNA and protein measurements are unchanged.
Explanation
The current evidence supports no detected functional effect under the tested conditions, not proof of no possible effect anywhere.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Record DNA event, genomic location, lineage, RNA/protein evidence, cell phenotype, population evidence, alternatives, and claim limit.

  • Deep intronic variant: A base substitution occurs far from known splice and regulatory regions; RNA and protein measurements are unchanged. The current evidence supports no detected functional effect under the tested conditions, not proof of no possible effect anywhere.
  • Recurrent functional tumour variant: A variant recurs in tumours, activates a growth pathway in cells, and its inhibition reduces growth in matched models. Converging recurrence and functional evidence supports a driver role in that tumour context.
  • Inherited risk variant: A validated germ-line variant raises disease probability but shows incomplete penetrance. The variant changes risk rather than guaranteeing disease, and counselling must address family information and uncertainty.

Lesson 21 · Molecular Genetics

Restriction Enzymes, Ligase, and Transformation

How can molecular tools cut, join, and introduce DNA sequences?

Required time
105 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C3.4k, C3.5k, C3.1sts, C3.2s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to explain how restriction enzymes, ligase, vectors, transformation, and selection support recombinant-DNA experiments.

Success criteria

  • I can trace DNA from source sequence through cutting, joining, introduction, and verification.
  • I can distinguish selectable marker, reporter, insert, vector, host cell, and expression evidence.
  • I can evaluate biotechnology benefit and risk without assuming that successful transformation guarantees correct expression or safety.

Retrieve

Build and verify

Why is inserting DNA into a vector not enough to prove that a host cell contains the correct sequence and produces a functional protein?

Not saved yet

Restriction

Sequence-specific enzymes cut DNA reproducibly

Restriction endonucleases recognize selected DNA sequences and cut phosphodiester backbones, producing sticky or blunt ends depending on the enzyme. Matching compatible ends can support controlled assembly. A recognition site can occur within an intended insert, so map design matters.

A restriction enzyme does not know which gene scientists want; it acts wherever its recognition and reaction conditions permit. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Ligation and vectors

A vector carries an assembled insert

DNA ligase seals compatible backbone breaks. Plasmid vectors can include an origin of replication, selectable marker, cloning site, regulatory elements, and inserted sequence. Insert orientation and reading frame matter when expression is intended.

A closed plasmid band or antibiotic-resistant colony does not by itself prove correct insert sequence, orientation, or function. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Transformation and selection

Cells must receive and retain the construct

Transformation introduces DNA into cells through method-specific processes. Selection allows cells with a marker to survive or be identified, while reporters can provide visible or measurable signals. Controls distinguish background growth, failed transformation, and construct-dependent effects.

Selection identifies a marker phenotype; it is not direct evidence for every part of the construct. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Verification and STS

Biotechnology claims need molecular and social evidence

Restriction analysis, PCR, sequencing, RNA measurement, protein assays, and functional tests answer different verification questions. Applications can include medicine, agriculture, research, and environmental work while raising issues of containment, off-target effects, access, ownership, consent, ecological spread, and regulation.

A responsible evaluation matches evidence to claim and identifies who benefits, who bears risk, and what monitoring can trigger revision. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Recombinant-DNA model

Diagnose three points where a cloning workflow can appear successful but fail.

Choose a case and select the verification test that answers the actual question.

Empty vector

Evidence
Colonies survive selection, but insert-specific PCR produces no product.
Explanation
The selectable vector entered cells, but the target insert is absent; vector-only background is plausible.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Map each claim—presence, orientation, sequence, RNA, protein, function—to a specific test and control.

  • Empty vector: Colonies survive selection, but insert-specific PCR produces no product. The selectable vector entered cells, but the target insert is absent; vector-only background is plausible.
  • Reverse orientation: Insert DNA is present, but transcript from the intended promoter is absent. Incorrect orientation or regulatory design can explain presence without expected transcription.
  • Protein inactive: Correct DNA and RNA are detected, but the purified protein lacks expected activity. Translation, folding, modification, sequence error, or assay conditions remain possible after DNA and RNA verification.

Lesson 22 · Molecular Genetics

DNA Evidence, Relationships, and Biotechnology

How can DNA patterns support identity, ancestry, diagnosis, and social decisions?

Required time
105 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C3.7k, C3.2sts, C3.3s, C3.4s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to interpret DNA patterns for relationship, identity, and biotechnology decisions while protecting uncertainty, privacy, and rights.

Success criteria

  • I can explain how PCR, electrophoresis, sequencing, and markers answer different questions.
  • I can compare DNA profiles probabilistically without saying a match proves identity or relationship by itself.
  • I can evaluate consent, database bias, family implications, data sovereignty, access, patents, and governance.

Retrieve

A match needs a reference

Why does a shared DNA profile pattern require population frequency, sample quality, and chain-of-custody evidence before supporting an identity claim?

Not saved yet

Molecular tools

Different methods produce different evidence

PCR amplifies selected regions, gel or capillary electrophoresis separates fragments, and sequencing identifies nucleotide order. STR markers can support identity comparisons, SNPs can support selected trait or ancestry models, and mitochondrial or Y-chromosome markers follow particular inheritance routes.

A method’s resolution, error rate, target, reference database, and sample quality define what it can support. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Profiles and relationships

Shared alleles change probability, not certainty

A DNA profile is compared across multiple markers. A match is evaluated against how common the pattern is in a relevant population and against related-source alternatives. Relationship testing calculates likelihood under stated family models. Identical twins, close relatives, mutation, sample mixture, and incomplete data can alter interpretation.

Say that evidence supports one hypothesis more than another; avoid “100 percent proof” when the statistic and alternatives do not justify it. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Biotechnology applications

DNA evidence can support diagnosis, treatment, ancestry, conservation, and research

Sequencing and marker data can identify variants, track inheritance, characterize organisms, monitor populations, or guide selected therapies. Validity and utility differ by application. An ancestry estimate depends on reference populations and model assumptions; it is not a complete record of culture, nation, kinship, or identity.

Clinical and identity claims need fit-for-purpose validation and professional context. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Rights and governance

Genetic data affects more than one person

DNA data can reveal health risk, biological relationships, ancestry signals, and information about relatives. Consent, secondary use, security, law enforcement access, discrimination, benefit sharing, patent or ownership claims, community governance, and Indigenous data sovereignty require explicit attention.

Technical capability does not create automatic permission. A responsible decision defines who controls data, how withdrawal works, and how benefits and harms are monitored. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

DNA evidence board

Compare three uses of DNA data with different interpretive and governance needs.

Choose a case and write the strongest evidence statement plus a rights safeguard.

Mixed profile

Evidence
A partial mixed sample includes alleles consistent with a person and with many possible relatives or unrelated contributors.
Explanation
The evidence cannot identify one source without mixture modelling, population frequencies, quality evidence, and alternatives.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Record question, method, sample quality, controls, comparison model, statistic, alternatives, consent, data control, and claim boundary.

  • Mixed profile: A partial mixed sample includes alleles consistent with a person and with many possible relatives or unrelated contributors. The evidence cannot identify one source without mixture modelling, population frequencies, quality evidence, and alternatives.
  • Relationship likelihood: A child and tested adult share marker patterns more likely under one stated biological relationship than under an unrelated model. The result supports the tested relationship model probabilistically and depends on reference, mutation, and alternative-relative assumptions.
  • Ancestry estimate: An algorithm assigns percentages that change after the company updates its reference database. The estimate is model- and reference-dependent and should not be equated with culture, citizenship, Indigenous belonging, or complete family history.

Lesson 23 · Investigation and Integration

Genetics Investigation Portfolio

Can a complete investigation connect model choice, data, uncertainty, and communication?

Required time
90 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C1.1s, C1.2s, C1.3s, C1.4s, C2.1s, C2.2s, C2.3s, C2.4s, C3.1s, C3.2s, C3.3s, C3.4s

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to design, analyze, and communicate a genetics investigation with variables, controls, uncertainty, and reproducible evidence.

Success criteria

  • I can turn a genetics observation into a focused testable question and justified method.
  • I can select a model, collect or use supplied data, calculate transparently, and compare alternatives.
  • I can communicate methods, safety, ethics, limitations, and revisions so another learner could audit the work.

Retrieve

Design before data

What makes a genetics investigation reproducible rather than a collection of interesting observations?

Not saved yet

Question and model

A good investigation connects mechanism to a measurable prediction

Begin with an observation and ask a question narrow enough to test. Identify independent and dependent variables, constants, sample or model population, and the genetic mechanism. Choose a chromosome, inheritance, molecular, or population model because its assumptions fit the question.

A hypothesis should predict a direction or pattern and explain why, not merely state that two variables are related. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Method and controls

Procedures must make comparisons interpretable

Define sampling, replication, measurement, classification, and data-recording rules before inspecting outcomes. Positive controls show a method can detect an expected result; negative controls reveal contamination or background. Blinding or randomized order can reduce observer and sequence bias when appropriate.

Use safe simulations or supplied data rather than biological samples from learners. Never collect family medical or DNA information. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Analysis

Calculations must remain traceable to raw evidence

Show counts, units, probability rules, expected values, graph scales, uncertainty, and any exclusions. Compare observed evidence with the selected model and at least one alternative. Statistical output should be interpreted in biological context rather than treated as an automatic truth label.

A significant difference does not measure practical importance or prove a mechanism; a non-significant result does not prove no effect. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Communication and revision

Reproducibility includes transparent limitations

A complete report links question, method, evidence, reasoning, conclusion, safety, ethics, and limitations. Distinguish planned from exploratory analysis. State which result would make the conclusion stronger, weaker, or require a different model. Peer or teacher feedback should improve traceability rather than reward certainty.

Sharing a method is not permission to share identifiable genetic data. Governance and consent remain part of scientific quality. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Genetics investigation board

Compare three investigation designs before accepting their conclusions.

Choose a design and identify the strongest repair.

No negative control

Evidence
A PCR investigation finds products in every tube, including unexpected samples, but no blank control was run.
Explanation
Contamination cannot be assessed; a negative control is needed before interpreting sample products.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

Score question, prediction, variables, controls, sample, raw data, analysis, alternatives, safety, ethics, and revision rule.

  • No negative control: A PCR investigation finds products in every tube, including unexpected samples, but no blank control was run. Contamination cannot be assessed; a negative control is needed before interpreting sample products.
  • Tiny ratio sample: Six offspring are used to reject a 3:1 model because the observed ratio is 4:2. The small deviation is compatible with sampling variation; a larger repeated sample and model check are needed.
  • Controlled model: A blinded synthetic dataset includes predefined variables, controls, raw counts, repeated samples, and an alternative model. The design supports auditable analysis, though model applicability and measurement uncertainty still require discussion.

Lesson 24 · Investigation and Integration

Integrated Genetics and Molecular Biology Case

Can chromosome, inheritance, and molecular evidence explain one unfamiliar case?

Required time
80 minutes
Optional extension
20 minutes
Outcomes
C1.1k, C1.2k, C1.3k, C1.4k, C1.5k, C1.6k, C1.7k, C2.1k, C2.2k, C2.3k, C2.4k, C2.5k, C3.1k, C3.2k, C3.3k, C3.4k, C3.5k, C3.6k, C3.7k

Materials and safety

Materials: The local evidence model, supplied synthetic data, calculator where useful, and the Investigation Notebook.

Safety: Use fictional, non-identifying evidence. This lesson cannot diagnose a genetic condition, disease, ancestry, identity, relationship, or individual health outcome.

Learning intention

I am learning to integrate chromosome, inheritance, DNA-expression, mutation, and biotechnology evidence in one unfamiliar genetics case.

Success criteria

  • I can organize evidence by chromosome, locus, sequence, RNA, protein, cell, organism, family, and population scale.
  • I can compare competing explanations and identify evidence that discriminates among them.
  • I can communicate a 95-quality conclusion with probability, rights, uncertainty, and a revision rule.

Retrieve

Do not jump scales

How will you prevent a chromosome image, pedigree, DNA variant, RNA value, and protein assay from becoming one unsupported story?

Not saved yet

Evidence architecture

Every result belongs to a scale and method

An integrated case can include karyotype, pedigree, cross, recombination, sequence, transcript, protein, cell phenotype, and population data. Record each observation with method, sample, units, time, quality, and scale. Separate direct evidence from calculated values and inferred mechanisms.

A finding at one scale does not automatically establish every later effect. Build the chain explicitly. Describe the pattern before naming a cause, connect each claim to a mechanism, and identify what another explanation would predict.

Model comparison

Different mechanisms can predict overlapping evidence

A phenotype could reflect chromosome number, one locus, many loci, regulatory sequence, splicing, protein function, environment, or interaction. A linked pedigree pattern can resemble sex linkage in a small family. A tumour variant can be driver or passenger. Generate alternatives before selecting one.

Discriminating evidence should differ between explanations, such as segregation pattern, transcript consequence, functional rescue, or matched control. Use the variables, units, timing, and comparison group to decide what the evidence supports; do not turn an association into a diagnosis or certainty.

Probability and uncertainty

Genetic explanations remain probabilistic

Punnett squares, likelihood ratios, recombination frequencies, penetrance, polygenic scores, and assay errors quantify different uncertainties. Report the denominator and reference. Do not combine percentages from unrelated models or replace an individual decision with a population average.

A precise number can still be biased, poorly calibrated, or irrelevant to the decision at hand. A defensible explanation separates observation from interpretation, names the biological scale involved, and states one limit on the conclusion.

Rights and communication

A complete answer includes governance

Genetic evidence can affect relatives and communities. A final recommendation should concern further evidence, counselling, monitoring, or governance—not diagnosis or treatment from a classroom case. Include consent, privacy, access, equity, cultural context, data sovereignty, and who can revise the decision.

Scientific strength is shown by traceability, mechanism, alternatives, and respectful limits, not by eliminating all uncertainty. When evidence conflicts with the first idea, revise the model rather than ignoring the result. Scientific quality depends on traceable reasoning, not confident wording.

Model Lab

Integrated genetics evidence board

Resolve three cases that require evidence from more than one Unit C module.

Choose a case and write the strongest cross-scale explanation plus next evidence.

DNA-to-RNA case

Evidence
A variant lies at a splice boundary, an exon is missing from mature RNA, and protein abundance is low.
Explanation
The sequence, RNA, and protein evidence converge on disrupted splicing; cellular and organism outcomes still require evidence.

0 of 3 cases inspected

Use the complete static equivalent

For each case, separate observation, calculation, mechanism, alternative, discriminating evidence, probability, rights, and revision.

  • DNA-to-RNA case: A variant lies at a splice boundary, an exon is missing from mature RNA, and protein abundance is low. The sequence, RNA, and protein evidence converge on disrupted splicing; cellular and organism outcomes still require evidence.
  • Pedigree and linkage case: A family pattern appears sex-linked, but a large test cross shows two autosomal markers inherited together with low recombination. Chromosome-location and linkage evidence support an autosomal linked explanation over the initial pedigree shortcut.
  • Cell-cycle and sequence case: A tumour carries many variants, but only one recurrent variant activates a growth pathway and predicts response in matched models. Functional convergence supports a driver role while heterogeneity and clinical response remain uncertain.

Use a model like a scientist

  1. Name the question. Identify the variable, population, process, or relationship.
  2. Inspect one case. Describe the evidence before choosing an explanation.
  3. Compare alternatives. Ask what another mechanism would predict.
  4. State the limit. Explain what the simplified model cannot establish.
  5. Save the reasoning. Carry useful evidence into an exit response or artifact.

Module evidence check: A PCR investigation finds products in every tube, including unexpected samples, but no blank control was run. Which interpretation is best supported?

Module evidence check: A family pattern appears sex-linked, but a large test cross shows two autosomal markers inherited together with low recombination. Which interpretation is best supported?

When an answer is wrong

  1. Read the targeted feedback and name the misconception.
  2. Return to the relevant model or evidence table.
  3. Explain why the selected distractor fails.
  4. Choose again only after revising the mechanism.

Reference workspace

Glossary and Data

Use precise terms to read models and evidence. Definitions explain how each term functions in this unit rather than replacing lesson instruction.

Unit C glossary

9:3:3:1 ratio

The expected phenotype ratio in a dihybrid cross when two genes assort independently and both show complete dominance.

A site

The ribosome site that receives the next aminoacyl-tRNA during translation.

ABO blood group

A human blood-group system controlled by multiple alleles in which IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive.

actionability

The degree to which a test result can support a useful, evidence-based decision or intervention.

addition rule

A probability rule for mutually exclusive alternatives: add the probabilities of the separate outcomes.

allele

One of two or more DNA-sequence versions at a gene or locus.

alternation of generations

A life cycle alternating multicellular haploid and multicellular diploid stages.

alternative splicing

Production of different mature RNA transcripts by combining exons from the same pre-mRNA in different ways.

analytical validity

How accurately and reliably a test detects the molecular feature it claims to measure.

anaphase

The division stage when separated chromosomes or chromatids move toward opposite poles.

aneuploidy

A chromosome number with one or more individual chromosomes added or missing rather than a complete set change.

anticodon

A three-nucleotide sequence on tRNA that pairs with a complementary mRNA codon.

antigen

A molecular feature recognized by an immune receptor or antibody; ABO antigens occur on red-blood-cell surfaces.

antiparallel

Describes DNA strands running in opposite 5-prime-to-3-prime directions.

apoptosis

A regulated form of cell death that removes selected cells without the uncontrolled rupture typical of severe injury.

asexual reproduction

Reproduction from one parent without gamete fusion, usually producing genetically similar descendants except for mutation.

banding pattern

The reproducible light-and-dark chromosome pattern used to identify chromosomes and some structural changes in a karyotype.

blinding

Keeping observers unaware of sample identity or treatment to reduce expectation bias.

blunt end

A double-stranded DNA end with no single-stranded overhang.

branch method

A probability method that multiplies along sequential branches and adds mutually exclusive final pathways.

cancer

A group of diseases involving abnormal cell growth caused by accumulated genetic and cellular-control changes in context.

carrier

In simple recessive inheritance, a heterozygous individual who has one recessive allele and usually lacks the associated phenotype.

cell cycle

The ordered sequence of cell growth, DNA replication, chromosome separation, and cell division.

cell plate

A plant-cell structure formed during cytokinesis that develops into new membranes and a separating cell wall.

centimorgan

A linkage-map unit corresponding to a one-percent recombination frequency, not a fixed physical DNA distance.

centromere

A chromosome region where sister chromatids remain joined and the kinetochore assembles.

chain of custody

A documented record of who collected, handled, transferred, stored, and analyzed a sample.

Chargaff's rules

The observed DNA base relationships that adenine approximately equals thymine and guanine approximately equals cytosine in double-stranded DNA.

checkpoint

A regulatory control point that can delay cell-cycle progression when conditions or molecular events are unsuitable.

chiasma

The visible physical connection between homologous chromosomes associated with an earlier crossing-over event.

chromatid

One DNA-protein copy of a replicated chromosome; joined sister chromatids separate during cell division.

chromatin

DNA together with associated proteins that package and regulate genetic material in the nucleus.

chromosome

One continuous DNA molecule with associated proteins and organized genes and regulatory regions.

cleavage furrow

The inward pinching of an animal cell membrane during cytokinesis.

clinical validity

How well a test result predicts or associates with a clinical condition in the intended population.

clone

A cell or organism descended asexually from one source and therefore highly similar genetically, though not necessarily identical in phenotype.

coding strand

The DNA strand whose sequence matches the RNA transcript except that DNA has thymine where RNA has uracil.

codominance

An inheritance pattern in which both alleles in a heterozygote contribute distinct detectable products or traits.

codon

A three-nucleotide mRNA sequence that specifies an amino acid or a translation start or stop signal.

complementary base pairing

Specific hydrogen-bond pairing of adenine with thymine or uracil and guanine with cytosine.

complete dominance

An inheritance pattern in which the heterozygote has the same scored phenotype as one homozygote.

controlled variable

A factor intentionally kept consistent so it does not confound the tested comparison.

converging evidence

Independent evidence types that support the same bounded explanation.

crossing over

Reciprocal DNA exchange between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during meiotic prophase I.

cyclin

A regulatory protein whose changing concentration helps control cyclin-dependent kinase activity during the cell cycle.

cyclin-dependent kinase

A protein kinase activated by cyclin binding that phosphorylates targets controlling cell-cycle transitions.

cytokinesis

Physical division of a cell's cytoplasm into daughter cells.

data sovereignty

The right of a people or community to govern collection, ownership, access, interpretation, and use of data about them.

deletion

Loss of one or more nucleotides or of a chromosome segment.

deoxyribose

The five-carbon sugar found in DNA nucleotides.

dependent variable

The measured response used to evaluate an investigation's prediction.

dihybrid cross

A genetic cross that follows inheritance at two loci.

diploid

Having two chromosome sets, conventionally written 2n.

diploid-dominant

A life cycle in which the multicellular diploid stage is the main body and the haploid stage is limited to gametes.

DNA

Deoxyribonucleic acid; the nucleotide polymer that stores hereditary information in most organisms.

DNA ligase

An enzyme that seals breaks in a DNA sugar-phosphate backbone by forming phosphodiester bonds.

DNA polymerase

An enzyme that builds DNA by adding complementary nucleotides to an existing 3-prime end and often proofreads the product.

DNA profile

A pattern of DNA markers used to compare biological samples; it is probabilistic evidence, not a complete identity record.

DNA sequencing

Determining the order of nucleotides in a DNA molecule or selected DNA region.

dominant

Describes an allele whose scored phenotype appears in a heterozygote under specified conditions.

double crossover

Two crossing-over events within the chromosome interval being studied.

double helix

The two-stranded helical structure of DNA with antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones and paired bases.

driver mutation

A somatic mutation that contributes causally to a cell's cancer-related growth or survival advantage.

E site

The ribosome site from which an uncharged tRNA exits after donating its amino acid.

epigenetic

Describes stable or regulated changes in gene activity that do not require changing the DNA base sequence.

evidence scale

The biological level and measurement context to which an observation belongs, such as molecule, cell, organism, family, or population.

exon

A transcript segment retained in a mature RNA after splicing, though not every exon segment is protein-coding.

expected count

The number predicted for a category by a specified probability model and total sample size.

expressivity

The degree or form in which a genotype-associated trait appears among individuals who express it.

frameshift

A reading-frame change caused by insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in a multiple of three within a coding region.

functional assay

An experiment that tests how a variant, molecule, cell, or process performs rather than only detecting its presence.

gamete probability

The probability that a gamete carries a specified allele combination under a stated genetic model.

gel electrophoresis

A method that separates charged molecules through a gel, commonly resolving DNA fragments mainly by length.

gene

A DNA region whose transcription contributes to a functional RNA or protein product, together with relevant regulation.

gene linkage

Tendency of loci on the same chromosome to be inherited together, especially when they are physically close.

gene order

The relative arrangement of loci along a chromosome inferred from recombination evidence or physical mapping.

gene-environment interaction

A pattern in which the effect of a genotype differs across environments or the environmental effect differs across genotypes.

genetic counselling

A professional process supporting informed understanding and decisions about genetic information, testing, uncertainty, and family implications.

genetic privacy

Protection of identifiable genetic information from collection, access, or use without appropriate consent and governance.

genotype

The allele combination an organism or cell carries at one or more loci.

genotype probability

The probability of a specified allele combination under the assumptions of a genetic cross or population model.

genotype-phenotype map

A model connecting genotype with possible phenotype while accounting for expression, development, environment, and variation.

germ-line mutation

A mutation in a gamete-producing lineage that can be transmitted to offspring.

goodness of fit

A comparison of observed category counts with counts expected under a stated model.

haploid

Having one chromosome set, conventionally written n.

haploid-dominant

A life cycle in which the multicellular haploid stage is the main body and the diploid stage is brief.

helicase

An enzyme that separates paired DNA strands at a replication fork.

hemizygous

Having only one copy of a gene or chromosome region in a diploid cell, as for many X-linked loci in XY cells.

heritability

The proportion of observed variation in a trait attributable to genetic variation within a specified population and environment.

heteroplasmy

Presence of more than one mitochondrial DNA sequence variant within a cell or individual.

heterozygous

Having two different alleles at a locus in a diploid cell or organism.

homologous chromosome

One of a pair of chromosomes with corresponding loci, one typically inherited from each parent, though alleles may differ.

homozygous

Having two copies of the same allele at a locus in a diploid cell or organism.

hypothesis

A testable proposed explanation that generates evidence-based predictions.

incidental finding

A potentially meaningful result discovered outside the original purpose of an analysis or test.

incomplete dominance

An inheritance pattern in which a heterozygote's measured phenotype differs from both homozygotes, often lying between them.

independent assortment

Independent orientation and separation of different homologous chromosome pairs during meiosis, producing independent allele assortment for unlinked loci.

independent event

An event whose occurrence does not change the probability of another event under the stated model.

independent variable

The factor deliberately changed or used to define comparison groups in an investigation.

insertion

Addition of one or more nucleotides or of a chromosome segment.

interphase

The cell-cycle period including G1, S, and G2, when cells grow, function, replicate DNA, and prepare for division.

intron

A transcribed segment removed from a pre-mRNA during RNA splicing.

joint probability

The probability that two or more specified events occur together.

karyotype

An organized display or description of chromosomes used to examine number and large-scale structure.

kinetochore

A protein complex assembled at the centromere that attaches a chromosome to spindle microtubules.

lagging strand

The new DNA strand synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments away from each advancing replication fork.

law of segregation

The principle that two alleles at a locus separate into different gametes during gamete formation.

leading strand

The new DNA strand synthesized continuously toward an advancing replication fork.

life cycle

The sequence of developmental and reproductive stages connecting one generation with the next.

likelihood

How compatible observed evidence is with a specified model or parameter value.

likelihood ratio

A comparison of how probable the same evidence is under two competing hypotheses.

locus

A defined chromosome position or DNA region used to locate a gene or marker.

map unit

A linkage-map distance equal to a one-percent recombination frequency; also called a centimorgan.

meiosis

A two-division process following one DNA replication that produces haploid cells and generates genetic variation.

meiosis I

The meiotic division in which homologous chromosomes separate, reducing chromosome-set number.

meiosis II

The meiotic division in which sister chromatids separate without another preceding DNA replication.

messenger RNA

An RNA molecule carrying a coding sequence from DNA transcription to a ribosome for translation.

metaphase

The division stage when chromosomes align at the cell's metaphase plate and attach to spindle structures.

microtubule

A dynamic cytoskeletal polymer that forms much of the spindle and moves or positions chromosomes.

missense

A coding-sequence change that substitutes one amino acid for another in a protein.

mitochondrial inheritance

Inheritance of mitochondrial DNA, usually through the egg cytoplasm in humans, with effects influenced by heteroplasmy.

mitosis

Nuclear division that separates replicated sister chromatids into genetically similar daughter nuclei.

mitotic index

The proportion of observed cells that are in mitosis at a particular time.

model assumption

A stated condition required for a model's predictions or calculations to apply.

model calibration

Assessment of whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies in an appropriate population.

monohybrid cross

A genetic cross that follows inheritance at one locus.

monosomy

Aneuploidy in which one chromosome from a pair is missing.

mosaicism

Presence of genetically distinct cell populations derived from one zygote within an individual.

multifactorial trait

A trait influenced by multiple genetic factors, environmental factors, and their interactions.

multiple alleles

Three or more allele versions present at one locus in a population, though a diploid individual carries at most two.

multiplication rule

A probability rule that multiplies probabilities along a sequence of independent or conditional events.

mutation

A change in DNA sequence; its effect may be neutral, harmful, beneficial, conditional, or not yet known.

mutually exclusive

Describes outcomes that cannot occur together in the same trial under the stated categories.

negative control

A comparison expected to lack the target signal, used to reveal contamination or background effects.

nondisjunction

Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate normally during cell division.

nonsense

A coding-sequence change that converts an amino-acid codon into a stop codon.

nucleotide

A phosphate, five-carbon sugar, and nitrogenous base; the repeating subunit of DNA and RNA.

observed count

The number actually measured in a category before comparison with a model.

Okazaki fragment

A short DNA segment synthesized discontinuously on the lagging strand and later joined by DNA ligase.

oogenesis

Development of female gametes through mitosis, growth, meiosis, and unequal cytokinesis.

origin of replication

A DNA region where replication begins and replication forks form.

P site

The ribosome site holding the tRNA attached to the growing polypeptide chain.

parental combination

An allele arrangement matching a chromosome combination present in the original parent, often more frequent than recombinant types in linkage crosses.

passenger mutation

A somatic mutation carried by a tumour cell that did not provide the growth advantage driving that tumour lineage.

PCR

Polymerase chain reaction; a laboratory method that uses primers and repeated temperature cycles to amplify a selected DNA region.

pedigree

A diagram of reported trait occurrence and relationships across generations, interpreted probabilistically and with privacy safeguards.

penetrance

The proportion of individuals with a genotype who show the associated phenotype under specified conditions.

peptide bond

The covalent bond linking amino acids in a polypeptide.

phenotype

An observable or measurable characteristic produced through genotype, gene expression, development, and environment.

phenotype probability

The probability of a scored characteristic after translating genotype possibilities through the inheritance model.

phosphodiester bond

The covalent linkage joining adjacent nucleotides in a DNA or RNA sugar-phosphate backbone.

Photo 51

Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling's X-ray diffraction image whose pattern provided important evidence about DNA's helical structure.

plasmid

A usually circular DNA molecule that replicates separately from a cell's main chromosome and can serve as a biotechnology vector.

ploidy

The number of complete chromosome sets in a cell or life-cycle stage.

polar body

A small haploid cell produced by unequal cytokinesis during oogenesis that usually does not become an egg.

polygenic score

A statistical score combining effects associated with many genetic variants; its usefulness depends on data, population, calibration, and context.

polygenic trait

A trait influenced by variation at many genetic loci, commonly also affected by environment.

polypeptide

A chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds that can fold or combine to form a functional protein.

positive control

A comparison expected to produce a known signal, used to show that a method can detect its target.

pre-mRNA

A newly transcribed eukaryotic RNA containing introns and exons before processing into mature messenger RNA.

primary oocyte

A developing oocyte that has entered meiosis I and may remain arrested in prophase I for years.

primary spermatocyte

A diploid germ cell that has replicated its DNA and enters meiosis I during spermatogenesis.

primase

An enzyme that synthesizes short RNA primers needed to begin DNA synthesis.

primer

A short nucleic-acid strand providing a free 3-prime end for polymerase extension and helping define the copied region.

promoter

A DNA region where transcription machinery assembles to initiate transcription of a gene.

proofreading

Detection and correction of some newly incorporated nucleotide errors during DNA replication.

prophase

An early division stage when chromosomes condense, the spindle forms, and nuclear organization changes.

proto-oncogene

A normal gene promoting regulated growth or survival that can contribute to cancer when abnormally activated.

Punnett square

A grid that organizes possible gamete combinations to calculate offspring genotype probabilities under stated assumptions.

randomization

Assignment or ordering by chance to reduce systematic differences and selection bias.

reading frame

The grouping of an RNA coding sequence into consecutive three-nucleotide codons.

recessive

Describes an allele whose scored phenotype in simple dominance is usually observed only without a dominant allele.

recognition site

A specific DNA sequence bound and cut by a particular restriction endonuclease.

recombinant chromatid

A chromatid containing a new allele combination produced by crossing over.

recombinant combination

An offspring or gamete allele combination different from the parental chromosome arrangements.

recombinant DNA

A DNA molecule assembled from sequences joined from different sources.

recombination

Formation of new allele combinations through crossing over, independent assortment, and fertilization.

recombination frequency

The percentage of recombinant offspring or gametes in a cross, used to estimate linkage distance up to a practical maximum of 50 percent.

reduction division

A division that reduces chromosome-set number, specifically separation of homologous chromosomes in meiosis I.

reference population

The defined population whose data are used to estimate frequencies, train a model, or interpret a genetic result.

replication

The semiconservative copying of DNA before cell division.

replication fork

The Y-shaped region where parental DNA strands separate and new DNA strands are synthesized.

reporter gene

A gene whose measurable product indicates whether a sequence, promoter, or cellular event is active.

reproducibility

The capacity for others to repeat or independently evaluate work using transparent methods, data, and analysis.

resolution

The smallest difference or structural feature a method can reliably distinguish.

restriction endonuclease

An enzyme that recognizes a particular DNA sequence and cuts the phosphodiester backbone at or near that site.

revision rule

A stated finding or condition that would cause an explanation, model, or decision to change.

ribosome

An RNA-protein complex that reads mRNA codons and catalyzes polypeptide synthesis.

RNA polymerase

An enzyme that uses a DNA template to synthesize a complementary RNA molecule.

RNA splicing

Removal of introns and joining of exons from a pre-mRNA transcript.

sampling variation

Chance difference between a sample result and the underlying probabilities or population because only a finite sample was observed.

secondary oocyte

The cell produced after meiosis I in oogenesis; in humans it is typically arrested in metaphase II until fertilization.

secondary spermatocyte

A haploid cell produced by meiosis I that proceeds through meiosis II during spermatogenesis.

selectable marker

A gene that allows cells carrying a vector to survive or be identified under selected conditions.

semiconservative replication

DNA copying in which each daughter double helix contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.

sex-linked

Describes inheritance of a gene located on a sex chromosome, most commonly discussed for X-linked loci.

sexual reproduction

Reproduction involving meiosis and fusion of gametes, generating new combinations of genetic information.

short tandem repeat

A DNA region containing a short sequence repeated a variable number of times and commonly used as a genetic marker.

single-nucleotide polymorphism

A common DNA-sequence variation at one nucleotide position in a population.

somatic cell nuclear transfer

A cloning technique that places a somatic-cell nucleus into an enucleated oocyte to begin development.

somatic mutation

A mutation arising in a non-gamete cell lineage that can affect descendant cells but is usually not inherited by offspring.

spermatid

A haploid cell produced by meiosis II that differentiates into a sperm cell.

spermatogenesis

Development of sperm through mitosis, meiosis, and cellular differentiation in the testes.

spermatogonium

A diploid germ-line stem or precursor cell that divides mitotically and can enter spermatogenesis.

spindle

A microtubule-based structure that attaches to and moves chromosomes during cell division.

spore

A haploid reproductive cell that can grow by mitosis into a multicellular haploid organism without gamete fusion.

start codon

A codon, usually AUG, that establishes the translation reading frame and specifies methionine.

sticky end

A single-stranded DNA overhang produced by staggered cutting and capable of complementary base pairing.

stop codon

An mRNA codon that recruits a release factor and ends translation rather than specifying an amino acid.

substitution

Replacement of one nucleotide or chromosome segment with another.

synapsis

Close pairing of homologous chromosomes during meiotic prophase I.

telomere

A repetitive DNA-protein structure protecting a chromosome end from degradation and mistaken repair.

telophase

A late division stage when chromosomes reach the poles and new nuclear organization forms.

template strand

The DNA strand read by RNA polymerase to synthesize a complementary RNA transcript.

test cross

A cross with a homozygous recessive partner used to infer an unknown genotype or gamete frequencies.

test-cross class

One offspring category in a test cross, used to infer the gamete type produced by the tested parent.

testable question

A focused question that can be answered with observable or measurable evidence under a feasible method.

tetrad

The four-chromatid structure formed when replicated homologous chromosomes pair during meiotic prophase I.

three-point cross

A linkage cross following three loci to infer gene order and map distances, including possible double crossovers.

transcription

Synthesis of RNA from a DNA template by RNA polymerase.

transfer RNA

An adaptor RNA carrying a specific amino acid and an anticodon that pairs with an mRNA codon.

transformation

Uptake and expression of external genetic material by a cell; in biotechnology it often introduces a plasmid into bacteria.

translation

Ribosome-directed synthesis of a polypeptide according to the codon sequence of messenger RNA.

trisomy

Aneuploidy in which a particular chromosome is present in three copies rather than the usual pair.

tumour heterogeneity

Genetic and functional differences among cells within one tumour or among tumours from different people.

tumour suppressor

A gene whose normal product restrains cell division, promotes repair, or supports apoptosis and whose loss can contribute to cancer.

two-point cross

A linkage cross following two loci to estimate recombination frequency between them.

unequal cytokinesis

Division of cytoplasm into cells of different sizes, as in human oogenesis.

vector

A DNA molecule used to carry and replicate or express inserted genetic material in a host cell.

X-inactivation

Early developmental silencing of most genes on one X chromosome in many cells of individuals with more than one X.

X-linked

Describes a gene located on the X chromosome and its associated inheritance pattern.

X-ray diffraction

A method that infers molecular structure from the pattern produced when X-rays scatter through an ordered sample.

Y-linked

Describes a gene located on the Y chromosome and transmitted through Y-bearing lineages.

A reliable data-reading routine

  1. Read the context, variables, units, and sample.
  2. Describe before explaining. Name direction, magnitude, timing, and variation.
  3. Calculate transparently. Show symbols, substitution, result, units, and checks.
  4. Compare mechanisms. State another explanation and discriminating evidence.
  5. Bound the claim. Identify synthetic data, assumptions, uncertainty, and what cannot be concluded.
